newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yield curve seen positive, if not for politics.
newsitem.headline: NZ yield curve seen positive, if not for politics.

text.p: Conditions may be ripening for New Zealand's inverted yield curve to finally turn positive, but political machinations are likely to put a spanner in the works, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Over the next three to six months there's a possibility that the curve could flatten right out or potentially go positive," said a bond dealer, who declined top be named.
With the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising rates in the United States, a sell-off in U.S. Treasuries looks to be on the cards, which would see New Zealand long bond yields rise.
Combine that with the anticipation of a domestic easing in short term rates early next year, and the long-negative yield curve could well turn its gaze skyward.

The Reserve Bank is widely expected to maintain its currently tight policy settings when it releases its September economic projections on Friday, but economists say it may not object if the market starts to nudge short rates lower.
Add to that the negative pressure that domestic political uncertainties are expected to put on longer bonds, and the prospects for a positive yield curve look decidedly good.
But New Zealand's new era of conciliatory politics could put a swift end to any chance of a more conventional yield curve.
On October 12, New Zealanders go to the polls for the first time under a new proportional representation system.
Highly conducive to coalition or minority government, the new system is likely to result in deals being cut between the major parties in order to win support and formulate a stable legislature.

Polls show the governing National Party is likely to remain the biggest party, but the opposition Labour, New Zealand First and Alliance parties look set to gain more than half of the seats between them.
"One thing that will probably occur after the election is that the (Reserve Bank's) target band will probably go from 0-2 to 0-3 percent," said another bond dealer.

The Reserve Bank is currently mandated to keep underlying inflation within a 0-2 percent band, but left-of-centre parties have indicated their desire to alter the range in order to alleviate the economic pressures of tight monetary policy.
"If they (the government) were in a position where they've got to negotiate with somebody else, a widening of the band would be one of the first chips on the table," the dealer said.
"So on that basis, we've got to up our projections on inflation a little bit, and that's why we can't really see a positive yield curve at this stage."
ANZ Treasury Economist David Drage agreed that a widening of the band would not necessarily see an easing in short rates and a positive yield curve.

"The problem is that if, say, soon after the election the band gets widened, we're not necessarily in any better position because September underlying inflation is likely to be around 2.6 percent, and that's getting fairly close to the top of (for example) a three percent band anyway," he said.
"While it would certainly help, that short end is still likely to remain quite considerably higher than the mid bonds."
He said the Reserve Bank's assumption that underlying inflation would retreat to around 1.0 percent in the first half of 1997 was "arguably optimistic".

"We could be looking at inflation at least at the top of the 0-2 percent band well into '97, paticularly if the Reserve Bank comes out an eases in early '97 as we expect," Drage said, adding that long bonds could also rally on a reasonably positive election result.
And because the election makes New Zealand's economic direction particularly unclear, the yield curve is likely to remain negative, for the time being at least.
